name: Curse of Knowledge
description: Once people know something, it becomes hard for them to reconstruct what it is like not to know it. Experts systematically overestimate what novices can infer, notice, or understand unaided.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to onboarding, information architecture, UX writing, and internal-tool design: expert teams ship labels, flows, and explanations that feel obvious to them but are opaque to first-time users.
prevalence_note: Common in product-writing, onboarding, and expert-review discussions ('you know too much to see what the novice sees'), even if it is invoked more as a design pitfall than as a formal bias label.

findings.description: Better-informed agents were unable to ignore private information fully when trying to reproduce the judgments of less-informed agents, producing the curse of knowledge. Market settings reduced the bias by about 50 percent, but did not eliminate it.
findings.effect_size: Market forces reduced the curse by approximately 50% but did not eliminate it
findings.source_title: The Curse of Knowledge in Economic Settings: An Experimental Analysis

applications.title: Elon Musk's internal memo banning acronyms and jargon at SpaceX
applications.description: Intercom's blog on writing clearly cites Elon Musk's real internal SpaceX communication policy banning acronyms and unnecessary technical jargon company-wide, explicitly because engineers steeped in daily technical work lose the ability to judge what a reader without that same immersion will and won't understand -- a direct organizational countermeasure to the curse of knowledge, not just an abstract writing tip.
applications.industry_context: aerospace engineering, internal corporate communication policy
applications.ethical_note: A deliberate organizational policy aimed at improving internal clarity and reducing communication friction, not a persuasion or dark-pattern technique aimed at external users.

applications.title: Newton's 'tapping study': tappers wildly overestimate how recognizable their tune is
applications.description: In her 1990 Stanford doctoral dissertation, Elizabeth Louise Newton had participants either tap out well-known songs by finger-tapping the rhythm on a desk ('tappers') or try to identify the song from the tapping alone ('listeners'). Tappers estimated listeners would correctly identify the tune about 50% of the time (with individual estimates ranging from 10% to 95%); in reality, listeners succeeded only 2.5% of the time -- far below even the most pessimistic tapper's estimate. Tappers, who could hear the tune clearly in their own heads, could not imagine how unrecognizable it was to someone without that knowledge.
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real, foundational, precisely quantified academic study, not a persuasion or product-design case -- there is no manipulator here, only a clean demonstration of how possessing knowledge (the tune in your head) makes it nearly impossible to accurately model what someone without that knowledge actually perceives.
